The flavour profile of this recipe is what I usually use for pork belly, I'd cook it slightly differently though. 180 deg C is too high for a slow roast. It works fine, but you will get much more tender meat doing it lower and slower.

I find the optimal temp for the majority of cooking is around 120 deg C, for between 3 to 6 hours depending on the thickness of the belly. A 1 kilo belly around 3 hours, a 2.5kg belly with bone in up to 6 hours. Cook longer if you like it to be pull apart tender, shorter if you prefer it to be more firm. If you have the time you can prepare it as below.

The changes I make are the following, this will give you a hard crunch crackling and tender meat:

  1. Start prep the night before. Score it as shown in the video, then pour boiling water over the skin. Pat completely dry with paper towel.

  2. Crush fennel seed with salt, black pepper and a couple of cloves garlic in a mortar and pestle. Make enough to cover the belly as you would salt a steak. Rub it all over and place in fridge overnight, preferably uncovered on a roasting rack, exposed to the drying air of the fridge.

  3. Take out of fridge an hour before starting cooking, turn on oven and pat belly dry again with paper towel. Lightly rub with a high smoke point oil like grapeseed or refined olive oil, not virgin or evoo.

  4. Do the vegetables and other spices as shown, but you really only want to brown for a minute due to the long cook time. Add a quarter the wine and stock instead of what is shown, bring to boil and take off heat. I like to add a couple of apples and brown onions to the mix. Too much liquid will create a very humid oven and lead to tough or chewy crackling. I like to reserve the green leaf from fennel for plating, makes a great tasty decorative element.

  5. Place pork belly on top of vegetables and cook for the 3-6 hours at 120deg C. Add in more hot wine/stock mix if vegetables look dry during cooking, ideally you want around 2 cm of liquid at base of pan. Do not baste.

  6. Remove pork belly from oven, place on roasting rack on flat tray with double layer foil underneath. Foil isn't necessary but makes cleanup a lot easier. Turn oven up to highest temperature fan forced.

  7. Process vegetables into sauce, you can leave it chunky as shown or remove the star anise and cardamon and blend smooth, just up to personal preference.

  8. When pork has been out for 20 minutes and oven is roaring hot place back in and wait for skin to bubble, watch carefully after a few minutes as to not overdo it.

  9. Take out, turn oven off, rest for 10 minutes. With a sharp filleting knife, remove crackling and place in oven with door open to keep hot and crispy while portioning the meat.

  10. Place meat on hot plate first, pour sauce over meat, then portion crackling over top. I like to serve it with a side of white cabbage and purple radicchio slaw with very thinly sliced raw fennel mixed in and rough cut blanched, air dried, then roasted rosemary/sea salt potatoes. Also spring greens with garlic butter and lemon zest with a bit of juice, if I can be bothered doing 3 sides.

This recipe is a mash up of Jamie Oliver and Ramsay techniques with tricks borrowed from Chinese and Italian cooks.

For special occasions and very large cuts I put in a bit more effort and start it two days before and use baking soda with white vinegar and 48 hours drying time, instead of the salt fennel seed mix which I only add just before cooking. This gives you a crackling similar to Chinese roast pork (Siew Yuk) instead of a BBQ style hard crunch crackling.

Been meaning to write that out for a while for friends and family, I was obsessed with the perfect pork belly meat and crackling when doing my apprenticeship. You can mess around with lye water, boiling vodka instead of water, etc, all will give you great crackling but personal preference will dictate your preferred method.
